summary:
The Longer Catechism, a standard Russian Orthodox statement of the faith, teaches that the Communion is a sacrament in which the believer, under the forms of bread and wine, partakes of the very Body and Blood of Christ to everlasting life. At the moment the words of institution are spoken in the Liturgy the bread and wine are changed, or transubstantiated, into the very Body and Blood of Christ; it adds, citing the Eastern patriarchs' exposition, that the word does not define how this happens, which only God understands. The catechism makes the Communion the chief part of divine service, asks believers to confess and communicate, and calls the faithful to receive at least once a year. The questions read do not address whether the Liturgy is a sacrifice.

The Orthodox Confession of Peter Mogila teaches that the Eucharist is the Body and Blood of Christ under the species of bread and wine, in which Christ is present really and properly. At the consecration the priest invokes the Holy Spirit and the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the substance of Christ's body and blood, so that the bread becomes the very Body of Christ and the wine his very Blood, with only the appearances remaining. Only a lawfully ordained priest may celebrate it, and it is given to clergy and laity in both kinds. The confession also says the mystery is offered as a sacrifice for all orthodox Christians, living and dead, and calls it a propitiation as well as a commemoration of Christ's death.

points.question: What is the Communion?
points.answer: A sacrament in which the believer, under the forms of bread and wine, partakes of the very Body and Blood of Christ, to everlasting life. It forms the chief and most essential part of divine service.

points.question: What happens to the bread and wine?
points.answer: At the moment the words of institution are spoken, they are changed, or transubstantiated, into the very Body and Blood of Christ. Citing the Eastern patriarchs, the catechism says the word does not define the manner of the change, which only God understands; it means the bread truly, really and substantially becomes the very Body of the Lord.

points.question: Who may receive, and how often?
points.answer: Anyone who desires to approach is asked to prepare, and the Church calls those who live religiously to confess to a spiritual father and communicate several times a year, requiring all to receive at least once a year.

points.question: What happens to the bread and wine?
points.answer: By the working of the Holy Spirit, called down on the gifts, the substance of the bread and wine is changed into the very substance of Christ's body and blood; only the visible species remain, so that the body is received by faith.

points.question: Is it a sacrifice?
points.answer: Yes. The priest offers the unbloody sacrifice, and the mystery is offered as a sacrifice for all orthodox Christians, living and dead. Its fruits include a commemoration of Christ's death and a propitiation for sins of the living and the dead.

points.question: Who may administer and receive?
points.answer: Only a lawfully ordained priest may administer it, even in urgent need. Clergy and laity alike receive both the bread and the wine.

review.note: The Longer Catechism: Questions 315-317, 322, 338-341 and 343 read in the azbyka.ru English text on 2026-11-12. The catechism's treatment of the Liturgy as an offering and of prayer for the dead was not read closely, so the sacrifice question is left "not stated" here rather than guessed; the Orthodox Confession addresses it. The rest of the section was not used. Not yet checked by a second reviewer. The Orthodox Confession: Questions 106-107 read in part on 2026-11-12 in the azbyka.ru English text; the later parts of the answer to Q. 107 (the remaining fruits and the honor due to the mysteries) were read only in outline. The numbering in the edition read repeats Q. 107. Date and the patriarchs' endorsement are from general knowledge and unchecked. Not yet checked by a second reviewer.
